This report introduces Vulcan, a 70-MW grid-interactive data center test platform developed in collab- oration with the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) and powered by NREL’s Advanced Research on Integrated Energy Systems (ARIES) virtual emulation environment. Vulcan incorporates a digital real-time simulation of Verrus data center design and integrates it with Verrus’ intelligent power flow management management system using a microgrid controller-hardware-in-the-loop (CHIL) frame- work. This enables rigorous testing of grid-interactive control strategies, real-time dispatch coordination, and system resilience behaviors under realistic electrical conditions. Vulcan was built to address the ques- tions being raised by system operators, planners, and policymakers today: How much can flexible loads actually help? Under what conditions? What capabilities must data centers develop to be part of the solu- tion? In the following sections, we explore these questions in depth, and we offer a blueprint for the next genera- tion of grid-interactive infrastructure that is ready for operational deployment today. 2 This report is available at no cost from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) at www.nrel.gov/publications 2 Vulcan Test Platform Overview Verrus’ data center design replaces traditional diesel generators with a BESS as the primary backup power source for both facility and information technology (IT) workloads during utility outages. Integrated with a 23-kV medium-voltage distribution system and advanced power flow optimization, the BESS also en- ables grid-interactive capabilities, such as demand response—transforming the data center from a passive load into an active, flexible asset that supports grid stability during peak demand periods. The medium- voltage power distribution architecture is agnostic to the type of backup power, and, as such, additional generators, fuel cells, or other units can be deployed as secondary backup to ensure that critical loads are maintained during extended grid outages. The medium voltage is converted to low voltage (415/480 V AC) through a step-down transformer to supply power to IT and associated cooling loads. Appropriate redundancies exist in the medium-voltage and low-voltage aspects of the power system to allow system availability higher than 99.99+ %. The system allows concurrent maintainability in all aspects of the electrical and mechanical infrastructure, with no single points of failure. Given the high uptime requirements, along with the goal of providing services to the grid, a dedicated control system is needed to manage the power flow. Verrus has developed a novel control system, referred to as the power flow management system (PFMS), that delivers operational data center functionality while enabling the data center to respond to requests from the grid. The PFMS design is inspired by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) open standards, such as IEEE 2030.7 [2] and IEEE 1547-2018 [3]; and it interfaces with/controls power hardware, such as BESS, generators, and switchgear relays. The PFMS also interfaces with higher-level systems, including supervisory control and data acquisition and tertiary control systems, such as Verrus’ optimal dispatch engine, but these are not a focus of this report and hence are shown as dotted interfaces in Figure 1.
